power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: For more than half a century, two traditions have addressed this problem in paralell: factor analysis and item response theory (IRT).

The factor analysis tradition investigates item quality via item loadings, communalities and uniqueness using the empirical correlation matrix, while IRT estimates parameters such as discrimination and difficulty, that define the probability of a response to an item as a function of one or more latent traits (Reckase, 2009; Wirth & Edwards, 2007).

text.text: The original network loadings partition the connections of the items or nodes across the communities estimated via EGA, producing an item-by-dimension matrix akin to factor loadings.

More recently, Christensen, Golino, Abad, and Garrido (2025) corrected the recovery of the network loadings signs, adjusted the within-community sum for the missing self-edge, and stabilized loadings magnitude across communities with different sizes.

text.text: With these developments, EGA moved from being a dimensionality assessment technique to a general methodology that can be used to describe where each item is positioned relative to those dimensions.

Based on the connection between IRT and full-information factor models, it is reasonable to think about using the EGA-based network loadings to estimate multidimensional item parameters in a network perspective.
However, in order to do this effectively, a problem needs to be addressed, i.e., the difference between a coordinate and a magnitude.

From a practical perspective, a researcher using EGA to identify the partition of the multidimensional space, and that wants to estimate multidimensional discrimination, intercept, or difficulty, needs to fit a separate multidimensional IRT model (MIRT; Reckase, 1997b Reckase, , 1997a Reckase, , 2009)), with its own estimator, rotation, and potentially its own allocation of items to dimensions.

text.text: Therefore, the parameters estimated following this procedure have no relationship with the structure estimated via EGA.

This apparent shortcut, i.e., to treat revised network loadings as standardized factor loadings and convert them into item response parameters, does not work, and the reason is quite straightforward. Christensen et al. (2025) shows that the magnitudes of network loadings are determined by: 1) the topology of the network, and 2) by the standardization used to compute the network loadings.

(2025)</ref> shows that the magnitudes of network loadings are determined by: 1) the topology of the network, and 2) by the standardization used to compute the network loadings.

text.text: Network loadings are not a by-product of the proportion of the variaance of the latent-response that the item shares with the latent dimensions, as in factor models or IRT.

Treating network loadings as factor loadings will generate three negative consequences: 1) inadmissible uniquenesses, 2) vector norms that depend on the coordinate system, and 3) duplicated normal-ogive-to-logistic conversions.

In summary, there is an indentification gap between the direction of an item in the space spanned by the EGA communities (identified by the network loadings) and the magnitude of its common component (which network loadings do not identify).
The current paper solves this gap by using a simple, but consequential, logical observation.

Since EGA can be used to estimate more than the partition of the multidimensional space, with the revised network loadings identifying the direction of every item in the multidimensional space, the only quantity that remains unindentified (from a factor-compatible latent-response model perspective) is one positive scalar per item that could generate the magnitude of the items.
That scalar can be estimated from the same correlation matrix that EGA uses.

Building on this observation, the current paper introduces the Directional Minimum-Distance calibration (DMD), a new estimator that keeps the EGA directions fixed and estimates a metric akin to item communalities by reproducing the observed off-diagonal correlations.
Analytically, it leads to multidimensional EGA-based discrimination vectors, intercepts, and scalar difficulties without the need to use a latent variable model (factor or IRT).
The aims of the current paper are threefold.
First, it explains the theory behind the DMD calibration method.
Then, the current paper presents an EGA-based multidimensional discrimination vectors, intercepts, and scalar directional difficulties.

Third, the current paper demonstrates that the factor carrying the uniqueness cancels from the difficulty, leading to a geometric interpretation as the location at which the response hyperplane of an item cuts the space spanned by the communities, termed in the current paper the community thresholds.
In this paper, DMD is evaluated in a Monte-Carlo simulation and compared to a exploratory Multidimensional Item Response Theory model with the correct dimensionality.

Two data generation mechanisms are used: the probit data-generating model favors the tetrachoric geometry used by EGA, while the logistic data-generating model favors the link fitted by the MIRT model.

The current paper also reports a very interesting consequence of the DMD equation: once the EGA directions are taken into consideration, the correlations betwen items factor into a product of item magnitudes, and as a consequence the relative magnitude of any two items is the same irrespective of which third item is used to compare them.
It is important to note up front that EGA-DMD is not proposed as a replacement for confirmatory MIRT.
It is a calibration method for those interested in obtaining item parameters after using EGA as a dimensionality assessment technique.
EGA-DMD can be seen as a bridge to classical item parameters under a factor-compatible latent-response model.

Under other data-generating mechanisms, such as the network models that motivate EGA in the first place (Epskamp, Maris, et al., 2018), the resulting values are calibrated summaries of the EGA geometry and should not be interpreted as the parameters of latent causes.

text.text: The simulation has two data generation meachnisms.

A probit latent-response model produces exactly the tetrachoric common factor geometry that EGA uses as its correlation target, while a logistic model produces exactly the link fitted by the MIRT model.
If only the probit condition were studied, the design would favor EGA, and if only the logistic condition were studied, it would favor MIRT.
Crossing both links therefore provides a direct test of robustness to reciprocal link misspecification.
The design also separates calibration from dimensionality assessment.

The MIRT model was given the correct number of dimensions, because the central question is the recovery of item parameters, while EGA was evaluated both with the generating item memberships supplied (a known-communities arm, which isolates the loading directions and the magnitude calibration) and in a fully empirical arm, which includes network estimation, dimensionality assessment, community detection, revised network loadings, and DMD.
Reporting both arms prevents error in community recovery from being mistaken for error in the calibration formula.

EGA-DMD and MIRT were also similar in recovering magnitudes and locations.

On average across all conditions, the communality RMSE of EGA-DMD was .040 and .038 of MIRT, the correlation between the estimated and generating discrimination norms was .966 and .970, and the difficulty RMSE was .066 and .063, respectively.

text.text: As was predicted by the reciprocal design, the data-generating link was responsible for which of the methods outperformed.

The current study, in addition to being inherently limited due to its sample-based nature, is constrained in several ways in terms of methodology.

First, the simulation included only 48 conditions with one 30-item bank with three dimensions, whose simple and cross-loading variants give a useful reciprocal comparison but do not span the entire factorial space of test lengths, number of dimensions, loading sparsity, discrimination differences and item difficulty.
Second, the study considered only dichotomous items.

The direction magnitude decomposition can be readily applied to ordinal latent response models: indeed, the several thresholds for one item share the same direction and communality, yet a separate derivation and study is necessary to extend DMD to this case.

Third, the exact population bridge holds only when the common factor representation is adequate and the EGA directions recover the directional geometry of the underlying factors; data generated by network models, on the other hand, need not satisfy Equation ( 18), in which case the DMD procedure becomes a minimum-distance summary of the EGA geometry, and the estimated item parameters should not be interpreted as the parameters of latent causes.

Directions of future research are discussed in Appendix I.
In this study, DMD calibration has been formulated, proven and simulated to estimate item parameters from the multidimensional structure found using EGA.
DMD possesses several features.
First, it maintains the EGA structure solution but uses only one more quantity, the magnitude of the items that the EGA does not provide.

Second, DMD is exact at the population level whenever the directions are correct, the factor carrying the uniqueness cancels out of its difficulties, and those difficulties were nearly as accurate as the difficulties of the full-information MIRT model in all conditions examined here.

Third, it is fast, reliable and clear, making it possible to analyze how much the magnitude estimation contributed to the item parameters obtained after the dimensionality assessment and direction estimation procedures.

The major disadvantage of DMD is also its main feature -the discrimination vectors of DMD are as accurate as directions it takes from the revised network loadings, which are different from the factor directions in case of cross-loadings.
Fixed-direction DMD also guarantees magnitude invariance under the exact fit condition.
Violation of this condition can be seen as an indicator of incompatibility of the correlation matrix and the estimated geometric structure.

In summary, DMD closes the gap between the EGA approach and the IRT theory, providing the natural item parameters calibration for the EGA and indicating the conditions when it corresponds to multidimensional item parameters.

text.text: A triangle of items is exactly identified, whereas a clique of four items has six correlations and four magnitudes and therefore supplies two independent tetrad equalities.
The TMFG starts from a clique of four items and adds one item at a time to a triangular face of the graph, so that the final graph is a chain of four-item cliques joined by shared triangles.
Suppose that every edge of the graph has a nonzero directional similarity and a positive direction-adjusted correlation.

If every clique satisfies its two tetrad equalities, each clique has a unique product factorization, and neighboring cliques agree on the magnitudes of their shared triangle, since a positive triangle identifies its three magnitudes uniquely.
The local factorizations then join into a single factorization over all the edges of the graph.

For J ≥ 4 items, the TMFG has 3J -6 edges and J -3 four-item cliques, which gives 2(J -3) independent restrictions on the logarithms of the direction-adjusted correlations for a fixed geometry, with the additional requirement that all the recovered communalities lie below one.

In this use, the TMFG only selects the pairs of items to be examined, and the direction-adjusted correlations are still computed from the latent-response correlations R ij , not from the partial correlations of the network.

Why should a researcher use EGA-DMD rather than fit MIRT directly?
Three reasons emerge from the present results.

First, EGA-DMD provides item parameters without replacing the dimensional solution already obtained with EGA, which avoids the situation in which a second exploratory model introduces a different axis solution or a different allocation of items.
Second, the calibration is fast and operationally stable.

EGA-DMD returned a solution for all but six of 12,000 datasets, its optimizer always converged, and it was several hundred to several thousand times faster than MIRT, whose convergence flag failed in more than half of the datasets at N = 5,000.
This speed makes EGA-DMD practical for bootstrap procedures, for large item banks, and for high-dimensional settings in which full-information estimation becomes expensive (Cai, 2010).
text.formatted: This speed makes EGA-DMD practical for bootstrap procedures, for large item banks, and for high-dimensional settings in which full-information estimation becomes expensive <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cai, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Third, the difficulties produced by DMD are nearly as accurate as those of MIRT in every condition studied, including those in which the directions are least accurate, so that applications that rely primarily on item locations, such as item selection or the construction of item maps, can benefit from EGA-DMD, whose difficulty recovery was consistently close to that of MIRT in the conditions studied.

When a factor model is known a priori to be the target and the precise orientation of the discrimination vectors is of primary interest, especially with cross-loadings, full-information or factor-analytic estimators remain natural choices.
The empirical illustration reproduced the central distinction between direction and magnitude.

The five EGA communities matched the content families in the selected item set, and DMD directional difficulties agreed almost perfectly with the confirmatory item factor analysis across admissible item comparisons.
With the composite coordinate correlations, the residuals were of similar size within and between communities, and no retained pair showed a sign discrepancy.

The CRT example made the boundary behavior concrete: the triangle formula flagged CRT07, the item with the highest DMD communality, as locally inadmissible without optimization, and the confirmatory model also identified Heywood cases.
The discount examples showed how different reference items can be used to examine magnitude separability directly.
Together, the examples demonstrate both calibration and model diagnostics within the EGA solution.
The probit latent-response model is exact for the tetrachoric geometry used by EGA, while the logistic model is exact for the MIRT model.

The results showed that the link had negligible effects on difficulty recovery for both methods and on the communality recovery of MIRT (η² p ≤ .02), and a medium effect on the communality recovery of EGA-DMD (η² p = .08).

Under the logistic link, DMD carried a small population approximation error, visible even with the generating directions, and MIRT gained a small advantage in communality recovery that grew with sample size.
Under the probit link, the advantage reversed.
In neither case did the link change the substantive conclusions.
The population EGA-native target was essential for this interpretation.

Evaluating sample EGA-DMD only against the parameters of the generating model would have confounded a difference between estimands with an inconsistency of the estimator, whereas reporting both targets showed that the population estimand and sampling variation provide distinct explanations for the observed finite-sample discrepancies.
Magnitude separability is an exact consequence of the fixed-direction representation (Proposition 2).

Once the EGA directions are divided out, the correlations between items factor into a product of item magnitudes, so that the relative magnitude of any two items is the same whichever third item is used to compare them, and the direction-adjusted tetrads vanish.

This result generalizes the vanishing tetrads of the one-factor model (Bollen & Ting, 1993; Spearman, 1904) to the multidimensional geometry estimated by EGA, and it resembles the specific objectivity of Rasch (1977), although it concerns item magnitudes within a fixed geometry rather than comparisons between persons, and it does not establish the axioms of additive conjoint measurement.

In the running example (Appendix D), the reference items that disagreed pointed to the same source of misfit that the residuals revealed in the empirical illustration, namely the slightly stronger associations between communities implied by the EGA directions.
The DMD communalities also quantify one of the two requirements for an additive person-item structure on the inverse-link scale, the other being a common item direction.
Which results should applied researchers inspect when using DMD with empirical data?
Four recommendations follow from the present study.

First, the stability of the EGA solution should be examined before calibration, for example with bootstrap EGA (Christensen & Golino, 2021a), because DMD inherits the communities and the directions of EGA.

text.text: In the present simulation, community recovery was nearly perfect, but empirical data with weaker structures may be less forgiving.
Second, the DMD residual matrix, E = R -ˆ︂ R, and the frequency of boundary communalities should be reported.

A communality at or near the upper bound indicates that the fixed directional geometry requires nearly all of the latent-response variance of an item to be common in order to reproduce its observed correlations, which is a warning to examine sampling uncertainty and compatibility of the fixed-direction representation, rather than a value to be silently repaired.

text.text: Several directions for future research follow from the limitations discussed in the main text.
The most immediate is the extension of DMD to ordinal items with multiple thresholds per item.

A second is the development of formal residual-based fit statistics and item-level misfit diagnostics for the DMD solution, possibly building on the entropy fit indices developed for EGA (Golino et al., 2021).
text.formatted: A second is the development of formal residual-based fit statistics and item-level misfit diagnostics for the DMD solution, possibly building on the entropy fit indices developed for EGA <ref type="bibr">(Golino et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A third is uncertainty quantification, which can be approached through bootstrap EGA, repeated network estimation, or a sandwich approximation conditional on the estimated directions.

A fourth is the development of an inferential test based on the directional tetrads of Proposition 2, possibly organized around the four-item cliques of a TMFG, whose sampling distribution must propagate the uncertainty of both the correlations and the estimated EGA geometry, together with the evaluation of the triangle formula of Equation ( 27) as a closed-form initializer for the optimizer.

text.text: A fifth concerns the directions themselves: because the results identified the coordinate correlation matrix and the remaining direction discrepancy under cross-loadings as the limiting factors for discrimination vectors, further improving the directional accuracy of network loadings in that setting would directly improve DMD.
Finally, the method should be evaluated with empirical instruments for which independent MIRT calibrations and substantive validity evidence are available.

Magnitude Separability
The fixed-direction representation that underlies DMD has a consequence that is not needed for calibration but that is interesting from a measurement perspective.

Once the EGA directions are divided out, the correlations between items factor into a product of item magnitudes, so that the relative magnitude of any two items is the same irrespective of the third item that is used to compare them.
In other words, the directional similarities estimated by EGA do more than supply the geometry required to identify the item parameters.
They also separate what two items share because of their positions in the latent space from what they share because of their magnitudes, and the second part has a simple multiplicative structure.

text.text: Three results stand out.
First, under the probit link, DMD with the generating directions reproduced every classical parameter exactly (communality RMSE ≤ .0001 in all six conditions).

Under the logistic link, the same directions produced small but nonzero discrepancies (communality RMSE between .011 and .014 and difficulty RMSE between .006 and .015), which quantify the cost of approximating a logistic item response function with the normal-ogive latent-response geometry.
Second, substituting the population revised network-loading directions introduced only a small structural discrepancy, which depended mainly on the loading structure.
For simple structure with orthogonal factors, the EGA directions coincided with the generating directions (mean row cosine of 1.000) and DMD remained exact under the probit link.

With correlated factors in simple structure, the mean row cosines were 1.000 and .999 for correlations of .30 and .60, and in the cross-loading structure they were .996, .998, and .998 for correlations of .00, .30, and .60.

Third, the magnitude-based parameters remained close to their classical values: in every population condition, the correlation between calibrated and classical discrimination norms was at least .990, the communality RMSE was at most .030, and the difficulty RMSE was at most .016.
Community recovery was perfect at the population level (adjusted Rand index of 1 in every condition), so that the known-and estimated-communities arms produced identical population values.

text.text: The contrast between the two methods is striking.
For MIRT, sample size was the only factor with a large effect on direction recovery (η² p = .88 for the row cosine), with only a small effect of the factor correlation (η² p = .04).

Taken together, the results of the section on DMD calibration in the main text show that DMD preserves three outputs of EGA, namely the detected dimensionality, the organization of items into communities, and the relative multidimensional direction of every item, and adds exactly one scalar magnitude per item.
It does not alter the network, reassign items to communities, or rotate directions to maximize agreement with any external model.
This separation has an important consequence for the evaluation of the method.

Any disagreement between DMD and classical item parameters can be decomposed into three sources: (a) a population difference between EGA directions and factor directions, (b) finite-sample error in the estimation of EGA directions, and (c) error in the calibration of magnitudes.
The simulation reported in the main text was designed so that each of these sources can be observed separately.

DMD is closely related to limited-information factor analysis: it minimizes residuals in an observed correlation matrix while holding the loading directions fixed, and with unit weights it is a constrained minimum residuals estimator (Harman & Jones, 1966).

EGA provides the dimensionality, the communities, and the directions, while DMD estimates only the unidentified magnitudes with the item response transformation following analytically.
